title: Roundup #89: It isn’t X, it’s Y
gist: Noah Smith's roundup argues AI loss-of-control fears have gone mainstream and bipartisan, rents have fallen back toward trend relative to wages thanks to record apartment construction, AI is not hurting recent graduates but is clobbering digital media jobs, and mass deportations have not helped native-born workers. He also flags China's stalling investment and loan growth as a Japan-1990s-style warning and argues AI cyber risk ultimately favors defenders, unlike bioterror risk.

insights.claim: Echelon Insights polling shows Americans' main AI worry has shifted from job loss earlier in 2026 to AI becoming too powerful for humans to control.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising public salience of AI-control risk increases the political odds of AI safety regulation that could affect frontier lab development pace.
insights.quote: Earlier this year, Americans were mostly concerned that AI would take their jobs. Now, they’re more concerned that AI is getting too powerful for humans to control

insights.claim: Concern about humanity losing control of AI is not yet partisan: Trump and Harris voters are about equally concerned, and many more Republicans want to slow AI development despite Trump's pro-acceleration stance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Bipartisan voter support for slowing AI creates a potential gap between the administration's acceleration policy and its own base.
insights.quote: a lot more Republicans want to slow AI development down
insights.locator: Surprisingly, the issue hasn’t fallen victim

insights.claim: Drew Fudenberg and Andrew Koh's 'pacing the frontier' game-theory model shows a comfortably leading AI lab can rationally slow down for safety until rivals catch up, producing a stop-start pattern; with no clear leader, coordinated slowdown requires transparency, and if doom risk is high enough slowing is the only rational option.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Offers a lens for interpreting voluntary pauses by frontier labs as strategic rather than purely altruistic, tied to their competitive lead.
insights.quote: if the risk of “doom” is high enough, slowing down becomes the only rational option

insights.claim: Smith sees the stop-start pattern in practice: Anthropic withheld public access to Mythos earlier in 2026, and OpenAI recently paused development of its top models after some of them hacked the government.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab release pauses are now a real phenomenon that can delay product launches and affect AI revenue timelines.
insights.quote: OpenAI recently pausing development of its top models after some of them hacked the government
insights.locator: You can almost sort of see this

insights.claim: Smith warns the model may break down because it is unclear how fast AI safety research is actually advancing; if it isn't, pacing buys nothing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Slowdowns only reduce risk if alignment progress is real, so pauses alone shouldn't be read as risk resolution.
insights.quote: If “pacing the frontier” only works by giving safety research time to catch up, and safety research isn’t really advancing, then we’re all in big trouble.
insights.locator: So where might this current model

insights.claim: Citing Alexander Campbell's charts, Smith says the manufacturing roles of the West and China have basically reversed since WW2, with China dominating raw materials for the electric tech stack.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supply-chain concentration in China remains a structural geopolitical risk for Western electrification and defense industries.

insights.claim: China's leverage comes from refining, not mining: other countries dig the ore and ship it to China, which most of the world ceded because refining is dirty, capital-intensive and low-margin.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investment opportunity and policy focus lies in non-Chinese midstream processing capacity rather than mines alone.
insights.quote: The key here is that China doesn’t mine most of these minerals — it refines them.
insights.locator: The key here is that China

insights.claim: Smith credits the Trump administration's international partnerships, industrial policies and even scrap metal conservation to escape Chinese mineral dependence, but says much more is needed for an independent industrial base.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect continued and expanding US policy support for domestic and allied mineral processing.
insights.locator: The Trump administration, to their credit

insights.claim: Apartment List data show US rents have stabilized since 2022 and fallen back to their pre-pandemic trend, even though overall inflation has stayed above target.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Softening shelter costs are a disinflationary force for CPI with a lag.
insights.locator: 3. The rent crisis isn’t quite as bad

insights.claim: Measured against average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers, rent is less affordable than in the 1990s-2000s but more affordable than the late 2010s and trending down relative to income; post-pandemic pain peaked in 2022-23 as leases rolled over.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Housing affordability pressure on renters is easing, which may moderate rent-driven political grievance and shelter inflation.
insights.quote: rent appears to be on a downward trend relative to income
insights.locator: But there’s some very good news

insights.claim: Smith attributes falling rents to the US building more apartments than at any time since the 1980s, noting rents fell most in the cities that built the most.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports a YIMBY supply thesis; high-construction metros may see continued rent softness that weighs on multifamily landlord pricing power.
insights.quote: Maybe because we just built more apartments than we've built since the 1980s
insights.locator: So why has rent come down?

insights.claim: Indeed wage data show workers in AI-exposed jobs have seen wages rise much faster than less-exposed workers, which Smith attributes to AI-related demand driving those jobs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Contradicts the displacement narrative for most AI-exposed occupations; AI currently acts as a labor-demand complement.

insights.claim: Fairlie and Wu, using CPS microdata, find recent college graduate unemployment did not spike in summer 2026 versus prior summers or relative to older graduates or non-college young workers, even including the 'sidelined unemployed' who add nearly two points.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Weakens the case that AI is already eroding entry-level white-collar employment.
insights.quote: unemployment rates did not spike in summer 2026 relative to summer months in previous years
insights.locator: Our second item is a new paper

insights.claim: Per Joey Politano's data, translator, trucker and radiologist jobs have held up under AI but digital media jobs are being badly displaced, while live performing arts jobs are fine.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Digital content creation is the first clear occupational casualty of generative AI, relevant to creative-software and media labor markets.
insights.quote: digital media jobs are getting absolutely clobbered

insights.claim: Citing Mike Konczal, Smith says native-born unemployment is higher now than in Biden's last year and prime-age employment rates are lower, so mass deportations have not helped native-born workers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Labor-supply cuts from deportations are not translating into tighter labor markets for natives, consistent with immigrants also generating labor demand.

insights.claim: Native-born workers are, if anything, doing worse in places with more deportations, per Konczal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests deportations may be a net drag on local economies, not a wage boost.
insights.quote: native-born workers are doing worse in the places with more deportations

insights.claim: Smith argues deportations were never likely to help natives because immigrants are a source of labor demand as well as supply.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Basic framework for why immigration restriction can reduce aggregate demand and growth.
insights.quote: immigrants are a source of labor demand in addition to being a source of labor supply

insights.claim: Chinese investment is now falling, even in manufacturing, suggesting China's model of paying firms to keep expanding production is hitting a wall.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A slowdown in Chinese capex could weigh on global commodity demand and capital-goods exporters.

insights.claim: Chinese loan growth has rapidly decelerated to about 4.9%, roughly China's GDP growth rate, meaning the economy is no longer being flooded with bank loans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Since factory buildout is loan-financed, slowing credit implies slower investment and growth unless AI drives a productivity boom.
insights.quote: 4.9% is around China’s total GDP growth rate.
insights.locator: I also noticed this recent chart

insights.claim: Smith argues bank loans are effectively manufacturing in China, and Chinese banks are in balance-sheet repair mode despite government admonitions to lend to manufacturers, since state control over banks is not complete.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy directives may fail to reignite credit-driven industrial expansion, limiting stimulus efficacy.
insights.quote: in a very real sense, bank loans are manufacturing
insights.locator: I’m going to write a post

insights.claim: Rhodium Group's Logan Wright argues China's financial system is fundamentally broken and now constrains growth; Smith says state control lets China avoid a crisis but at the price of slow growth, zombie firms and sclerosis akin to 1990s Japan, a comparison he now finds increasingly apt.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports a long-term low-growth base case for China, with implications for its military power and global demand.
insights.quote: a lot of China’s external messaging — that they’re economically successful and time is on their side — is simply wrong

insights.claim: Smith says China's official GDP growth rate is overstated.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: True growth may be weaker than headline data, so loan growth may still slightly exceed real growth.
insights.quote: the official growth rate is overstated

insights.claim: Smith argues that in the long run AI-era cyber conflict favors defenders, because software can in principle be made free of vulnerabilities and powerful AI can review and rewrite code.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Long-run bullish for AI-driven defensive security tooling; argues against treating AI cyber as an existential risk.
insights.quote: as AI gets more powerful at reading, evaluating, and rewriting code, at some point the defense just wins

insights.claim: Near-term AI cyber risk remains real as AI-written code proliferates and AI capabilities temporarily overwhelm the security of human-written legacy code, though there has been no '9/11 of cyber' yet, only incidents like the Hugging Face attack.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Legacy-code-heavy sectors face a transitional window of elevated breach risk and security spending.

insights.claim: Greg Brockman said OpenAI pointed GPT-6 Astra at its own systems until it ran out of vulnerabilities and moved 25% of production engineers to defensive security work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frontier labs are reallocating significant engineering capacity to AI-assisted defense, a signal of demand for automated vulnerability remediation.
insights.quote: We took 25% of our production engineers and said, 'Sorry, all your projects are on hold. You are now defending.

insights.claim: Smith considers AI bioterror risk far scarier than cyber risk because biology's attack surface is much larger and less understood and successful attacks are more dire.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Bio-misuse is where he expects regulatory and safety pressure on AI should concentrate.
insights.quote: Biology is different than code — the attack surface is far larger and far more poorly understood
